extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students in discrete mathematics or introductory programming (instructor notes also address intermediate/advanced courses)
extracted.subtask_description: A multi-part undergraduate project on Turing machines and computability: learn definitions (automatic/computing/circle-free machines), design specific Turing machines, work with standard descriptions and the universal machine, and study the Entscheidungsproblem via construction/diagonalization and proofs by induction/recursion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Automatic machine (a-machine)
rubrics_metrics.description: If at each stage the motion of a machine (in the sense of (1)) is completely determined by the configuration, we shall call the machine an 'automatic machine' (or a-machine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the formal condition that no external choices are required during operation; contrasts with choice machines (c-machines) which require an external operator when an ambiguous configuration is reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Computing machine
rubrics_metrics.description: If an a-machine prints two kinds of symbols, of which the first kind (called figures) consists entirely of 0 and 1 (the others being called symbols of the second kind), then the machine will be called a computing machine. If the machine is supplied with a blank tape and set in motion, starting from the correct initial m-configuration the subsequence of the symbols printed by it which are of the first kind will be called the sequence computed by the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The real number whose expression as a binary decimal is obtained by prefacing this sequence by a decimal point is called the number printed by the machine. Only output symbols of the first kind contribute to the computed sequence; symbols of the second kind serve as 'rough notes'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention: F-squares and E-squares (alternate squares)
rubrics_metrics.description: The convention of writing the figures only on alternate squares is very useful: I shall always make use of it. I shall call the one sequence of alternate squares F-squares, and the other sequence E-squares. The symbols on E-squares will be liable to erasure. The symbols on F-squares form a continuous sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use F-squares to store the continuous sequence of figures (output); E-squares are for temporary 'rough notes' and may be erased. There is no need to have more than one E-square between each pair of F-squares; apparent needs for more E-squares can be satisfied by richer symbol sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Circular vs circle-free machine
rubrics_metrics.description: If a computing machine never writes down more than a finite number of symbols of the first kind, it will be called circular. Otherwise it is said to be circle-free. A machine will be circular if it reaches a configuration from which there is no possible move, or if it goes on moving and possibly printing symbols of the second kind, but cannot print any more symbols of the first kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sequence is computable if it can be computed by a circle-free machine; a number is computable if it differs by an integer from the number computed by a circle-free machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard form for configuration tables and Standard Description (S.D.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables can be put in a standardized form so that each operations entry is one of specified simple forms (E; E; R; L; P α; P α, R; P α, L; R; L; or empty). Assign numbers to m-configurations q1...qR and symbols S0...Sm and reduce each line to one of three forms (.N1/, .N2/, .N3/). From each line form expressions qi Sj Sk L qm (or R or N) and write them separated by semicolons. Replace qi by 'D' followed by 'A' repeated i times and Sj by 'D' followed by 'C' repeated j times. This gives the standard description (S.D.), made from letters A, C, D, L, R, N and ';'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each instruction in the S.D. consists of five consecutive parts: (i) D + A^i describing m-configuration; (ii) D + C^j describing scanned symbol; (iii) D + C^k describing symbol to change into; (iv) L/R/N for movement; (v) D + A^m describing final m-configuration. Every instruction should be followed by a semi-colon when writing the S.D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Describe the workings of a Turing machine (1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the workings of a Turing machine (referred to as a 'computing machine' in the original paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the tape, squares, scanned square, scanned symbol, m-configurations, configuration pair (qn, S.r/), operations (write, erase, move left/right, change m-configuration), the notion of complete configuration and moves. Reference Turing's original exposition as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Determine precise output of Example 1 (1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the precise output of the machine in Example 1? Certain squares may be left blank. Be sure to justify your answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully follow the machine's configuration table and operations, track printed symbols (figures) on F-squares vs E-squares, and justify why blanks remain or are erased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Design machine to generate specific sequence (1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design a Turing machine which generates the following output: 010010100101001... Provide justification for your answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce a configuration table (m-configurations and behavior) that yields the required infinite output pattern; show why it produces the pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Describe behavior of given machine (1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the behavior of the following machine, which begins with a blank tape, with the machine in configuration ˛. (Given a configuration table with operations and final m-configurations.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace operation row-by-row for given scanned symbols and show transitions, halting conditions, and final tape content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Design machine to test A ⊆ B with specified tape format (1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given finite non-empty sets A and B encoded on the tape as: 0 [elements of A] & [elements of B] Z (0, &, Z distinct and not in A or B) with the machine starting at the far left reading 0, design a Turing machine which tests whether A ⊆ B. The machine should erase all the elements of A if A ⊆ B and return a tape with blanks for every square which originally contained an element of A. You may use operations R, L, S (store one scanned character), C (compare scanned char with stored), E (erase), P( ) (print). You may use multiple operations per configuration and the word 'other' to denote all unspecified symbols. Machine must halt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a configuration table that systematically checks each element of A against elements of B (using the store-and-compare operations), erases originals of A if matched, and halts. Justify correctness and halting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise group: Trace outputs and prove pattern by induction (2.1–2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a more complex machine that repeats transitions among configurations a,b,c,... determine the precise output as the machine finishes configuration a and enters b for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, ... n-th time. Use induction to prove the general pattern; write careful induction details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the outputs at the first few occurrences, conjecture the general form, and provide a formal induction verifying the machine's behavior across iterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Design multiplication machine and verify by induction (2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design a Turing machine which, given two natural numbers n and m encoded as runs of 1's between markers A, B, C on the tape (A 1^n B 1^m C), computes their product so that the final tape contains between C and D exactly n·m ones. Machine starts scanning at A. Use induction to verify the machine's correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the configuration table for the multiplier T, show T(n,1)=n and T(n,m)=T(n,m-1)+n (recursive/inductive specification), and prove by induction that the machine produces the correct number of ones between C and D and halts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Compute outputs and S.D. for machine T (3.1–3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given machine T (configuration table provided), determine its output with a blank tape starting in configuration a (3.1). Rewrite the output using the 'standard description' for output symbols replacing each Sj with D C^j (3.2). Find the standard description (S.D.) of machine T, ensuring every instruction is followed by a semi-colon (3.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully translate each table line to the normalized forms and then to the D/A/C encoding; ensure correctness of the S.D. string and punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Universal machine setup with S.D. on a second tape (3.4–3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose #m-configurations ≤ 9 and #symbols ≤ 4. Write the standard description of some machine M on every other square (F-squares) of a second tape, with each instruction followed by a semi-colon and final '::'. Initially other squares blank. If the standard description for machine I (or machine T) is entered, analyze the output of the universal-like machine U (given partial configuration list) and compare with actual output of I (or T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulate U's given initial configurations and account for notation 20R, 10R shorthand. Compare coded output with M's actual output, taking into account symbol-coding conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Describe operations of U's initial configurations (3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe in words the operation of configuration one from machine U and separately describe the operations of configurations two, three, and four.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear informal descriptions of the listed configurations' roles (e.g., moving to find delimiters, printing markers, updating recorded state) referencing the provided operation list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Outline remaining operations of U and discuss recursion (3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning with configuration 17, outline the remaining operations of U so that U, when supplied with the S.D. of a machine M, will output the same sequence as M (coded by S.D.). U keeps track of M's current configuration in the first 18 squares after '::' and records M's scanner position via a symbol 'T'. Use phrases like 'match m-configuration', 'match scanned symbol', 'move scanner for M', etc. Does recursion occur in your outline?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You do not need to design an actual machine; provide a detailed procedural outline covering matching instructions, updating the simulated tape and scanner, and coding/decoding steps. Discuss whether this outline uses recursion (conceptually or via repeated simulation loops).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Produce actual machine instructions of U from configuration 17 (3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning with configuration 17, find the actual machine instructions of U so that U finds a match between an arbitrary configuration stored on the 18 squares to the right of '::' and a configuration at the beginning of a coded instruction to the left of '::'. Suppose the S.D. entered is that of a machine M for which there is always a well-defined next configuration. Use only operations 'R', 'L', 'E', 'P( )', and 'none', explain the new steps of U, and identify the present-day terminology used to describe U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce concrete instruction lines (normalized forms) that implement pattern matching between the 'current configuration' recording and the instructions on the left. Explain each added step. Present-day terminology: universal Turing machine / interpreter / simulator (explain correspondences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Determine circle-free status of given machines (4.1–4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given configuration tables for machines T1 and T2 (starting in m-configuration a with blank tape), determine whether each machine is circle-free. Justify your answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether each machine prints infinitely many first-kind symbols (0/1) or reaches a configuration with no possible move or can no longer print first-kind symbols; provide rigorous justification from the transition table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Explain distinguishing feature of circle-free vs circular machines (4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe in your own words the key feature which distinguishes a circle-free machine from a circular machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain in terms of the ability to print infinitely many first-kind symbols and avoidance of configurations with no possible moves; cite Turing's characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Computability of a specific sequence and construction/proof (4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the sequence 101001000100001... computable? If so, find a circle-free machine (with finitely many m-configurations) that computes this sequence on every other square (F-squares) of a blank tape. If not, prove no circle-free machine can compute it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either provide an explicit finite-configuration machine that produces the sequence on F-squares and argue why it is circle-free, or give a proof of non-computability (e.g., by contradiction/diagonalization) if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Cardinality of computable sequences and consequences (4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the number of computable sequences finite or infinite? If infinite, find a one-to-one correspondence between the natural numbers ℕ and a subset of the computable sequences. Use this to explain why a certain machine H must be circle-free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that computable sequences are countable (enumerable) via enumeration of machine descriptions (S.D.), and explain why a constructed H (which enumerates or uses diagonalization) cannot be circular, using listed properties of H.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Can machine H compute the diagonal sequence β0? (4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose H is constructed to compute the sequence β0(n) = f_n(n) where f_n is the n-th computable sequence. If H is circle-free and its sequence is among the enumerated sequences at index N0, explain how β0(N0) should be computed. Is it possible to construct machine H? If not, which component (D or U) cannot be constructed? Justify your answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss the diagonal argument showing contradiction if H existed; analyze constructibility of D (tester for circularity) vs U (universal machine) and justify which cannot exist so as to avoid contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Does the universal machine solve the decision problem? (4.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the universal computing machine solve the decision problem (Entscheidungsproblem)? Explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the universal machine can simulate any computable process but cannot decide provability/halting for arbitrary machines due to diagonalization/undecidability; tie to Turing's negative answer to Hilbert's decision problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise: Identify modern name for the decision problem (4.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: By what name is the decision problem known today in computer science? Support your answer with excerpts from outside sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate that the decision problem is related to decidability/entailment and in modern terms maps to questions like the 'halting problem' and general undecidability of first-order predicate calculus; cite authoritative sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor guidance: assignment scope and course suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes for the instructor: the project contains four sub-projects ('An Introduction to Turing Machines', 'Turing Machines, Induction and Recursion', 'The Universal Computing Machine', 'The Decision Problem'). The first two are ideal for an introductory undergraduate course and could be assigned as a separate two-week project; the second could be assigned while covering inductive/recursive constructions. The latter two sub-projects are suited for advanced/intermediate courses in discrete mathematics, logic, or programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the first two sub-projects for introductory students (two-week assignment suggested); use the latter two for more advanced students when covering computability/logic. An alternate variant: Turing Machines and Binary Addition (web resource referenced). Extra credit suggests implementing a universal computing machine in a programming language and demonstrating examples.
